title: Sūryaś ca mā: the water sipped at the morning worship
theme: The morning counterpart of 10.31: Sūrya and the powers over anger are asked for protection, the night’s wrongs are left to the night, and what remains is offered into the sun, the light.

words.context: Bhāskara: «सूर्य उपक्रान्तस्य अह्नोऽधिपतिः» — the lord of the day now beginning
Sāyaṇa: «क्रोधाभिमानी देवः» — the deity of anger; Bhāskara: «मननशीलमन्तःकरणं» — the thinking inner faculty
Sāyaṇa: «क्रोधस्वामिनस्तन्नियामका देवाः» — the deities who govern anger
Sāyaṇa: «मदीयकोपनिष्पादितेभ्यः» — brought about by my anger

words.role: ablative of what one is protected from

words.context: Bhāskara: «रात्रिया कृतं पापं रात्रिरवलुम्पत्विति विशेषः» — the night is to wipe out what was done by night
Sāyaṇa: «मरणरहिते जगत्कारणे» — the deathless cause of the world
The anonymous commentator: «सूर्येऽहर्निष्पादके सूर्योपाधिके» — the sun that makes the day, Brahman with the sun as its limiting adjunct

sandhi.rule: pāpam akārṣam: the m is joined to the vowel.
kim + ca → kiñ ca: m becomes the nasal of the following stop (P. 8.4.59 (वा पदान्तस्य)).
idam aham, mām amṛtayonau: m joined to the following vowel; aham before m is written with anusvāra.
A visarga becomes ś before c: sūryaḥ + ca → sūryaś ca.

sandhi.type: final t voiced before a voiced consonant
visarga before t; final t voiced
sandhi.rule: rātriḥ + tat → rātris tat; tat + avalumpatu → tad avalumpatu.

morphology.note: Instrumental of śiśna with the Vedic ending -ā for -ena; Bhāskara names the rule: «सुपां सुलुक् इत्याकारः».
First person singular of the s-aorist of √kṛ: ‘I have done’.

A Vedic instrumental of rātri, ‘by night’, with -iyā for classical rātryā; the same form recurs in 10.34 (rātriyāt). The anonymous commentator calls such forms Vedic usages («एते छान्दसाः प्रयोगाः», on 10.34).

translation.literal: May Sūrya and manyu and the lords of manyu protect me from sins done through manyu. Whatever sin I have done by night — by mind, by speech, by the hands, by the feet, by the belly, by the sexual organ — may the night wipe that out. Whatever wrong [is] in me, this [and] myself I offer into the source of immortality, into the sun, into the light. Svāhā.
translation.readable: May the Sun, and anger, and the powers that rule anger guard me from the wrongs that anger brings. Whatever wrong I did in the night — in thought, in word, with hands or feet, by appetite or desire — may the night that has passed wipe it away. Whatever wrong remains in me, I offer it, and myself with it, into the source of deathlessness, the sun, the light. Svāhā.

syntax: A wish in the third person imperative (rakṣantām), with three subjects joined by ca and an ablative of what is guarded against. Then a relative clause (yad … akārṣam) with six instrumentals of the means, resumed by tad and a second imperative (avalumpatu). The last sentence turns to the first person: a relative clause (yat kiṃ ca … mayi) and a main clause idam ahaṃ māṃ … juhomi with three locatives of where the offering is made.

ambiguities.note: Anger (Sāyaṇa, the anonymous commentator, and Bhāskara’s alternative) or the thinking inner faculty (Bhāskara’s first reading).

Sāyaṇa reads it as protection by removing sins already done («पापिनं मां तत्पापविनाशनेन पालयन्तु»); Bhāskara as protection from sins not yet done, ‘as one guards a house against thieves’ (see commentary).

The evening mantra offers ‘into the true’ (satye); this one ‘into the sun’. The anonymous commentator reads the sun as Brahman known through the sun («सूर्योपाधिके»); Bhāskara as the lord of the day now beginning.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: The pattern of 10.31 (which Bhāskara analyses), with rātriyā for ahnā: as printed the nine lines count 18, 6, 9, 8, 8, 8, 8, 10 and 10 syllables; the third line has one more than in the evening mantra because rātriyā has three syllables.

beginner: This is the prayer for sipping water at the morning worship. It repeats the evening prayer of the previous section with three changes. The Sun takes the place of Fire as the first protector; the wrongs to be wiped away are those done during the night, and the night that has just ended is asked to take them; and the speaker offers what remains, and himself, ‘into the sun, the light’. The old commentators say little more than that: one of them says the whole is explained as before, and another explains that the sun is named because it rules the day that is beginning. Together with the noon and evening prayers, it frames the day in three short reviews.
analogy: Like opening a shop in the morning: the night’s mess is swept out first, so the day starts clean.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The words of 10.31 with three changes: Sūrya for Agni, the sin done ‘by night’ wiped out by the night, and the offering made ‘into the sun, into the light’.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: «प्रातःसंध्याकाले जलपानार्थं मन्त्रमाह» — the mantra for drinking water at the morning worship; Sāyaṇa has the same sentence. Bhāskara: «सूर्यश्चेति प्रातराचमनीयम्».

commentary.q: How do the commentators explain the changes?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator explains only ‘the sun’, as Brahman with the sun as its adjunct, and refers the rest to the evening mantra: «सूर्येऽहर्निष्पादके सूर्योपाधिके। अन्यत्सर्वं पूर्ववद्ध्याख्येयम्». Bhāskara makes the sun the lord of the day that is beginning («सूर्य उपक्रान्तस्य अह्नोऽधिपतिः»), notes that the night is to wipe out the night’s sin, and that the offering is made into the lord of the day («उपक्रान्तस्यान्ह्नोऽधिपतौ होमः») — as in the evening the offering was made into Agni, lord of the night.

commentary.q: Where do the word glosses come from?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Both commentators send the reader back to the evening mantra («अन्यत्सर्वं पूर्ववद्ध्याख्येयम्»), so the glosses in the word table are taken from Sāyaṇa’s comment on 10.31 (his anuvāka 24): manyu as the deity of anger, the source of immortality as the deathless cause of the world («मरणरहिते जगत्कारणे»). The Vedic instrumental rātriyā is of the kind the anonymous commentator calls Vedic usages when it recurs in 10.34 («एते छान्दसाः प्रयोगाः»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Tirupati e-text omits जुहोमि and reads अमृतयोनी; the Ānandāśrama text misprints मन्युकृतैभ्यः. All are classified as witness errors (sources page).

schools.disagreement: No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. Bhāskara takes the sun simply as the lord of the day; the anonymous commentator as Brahman through the sun.

contemporary.text: The morning prayer does not carry the night forward: what was done is named and left with the night. Starting a day by deliberately setting down the previous one is a habit many traditions and many people find useful. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What would you want to leave behind with the night before starting a day?
reflect.deeper: Why might the morning mantra make the sun, and the evening one ‘the true’, the place of offering?
reflect.practice: On waking, take one breath to name anything from yesterday you want to set down before the day begins.

references.text: Sāyaṇa’s comment on this anuvāka (his 25) is the same short sentence as the anonymous commentator’s.

flags.note: The edition’s computed map sends Bhāskara’s anuvāka 24 to this anuvāka; his comment on it is in his anuvāka 25 («सूर्यश्चेति प्रातराचमनीयम्»), cited here explicitly.
